one_liner: SIMD 14-way probing hash map (F14) in Facebook's Folly library; 2-4x faster build/find/churn, 16x faster iteration than std::unordered_map.
what_it_does: F14 is Folly's hash-table family with three storage policies sharing one probing core: F14ValueMap stores key/value pairs inline (fastest, no reference stability), F14NodeMap heap-allocates each entry like std::unordered_map (same iterator/reference stability, safe drop-in), and F14VectorMap packs values in a separate contiguous array (best for large keys/tables). F14FastMap auto-selects ValueMap or VectorMap by entry size. All variants support heterogeneous/transparent lookup (e.g. querying a std::string-keyed map with a StringPiece) without constructing the key type, and most of the unordered-associative-container API, though bucket-level functions and max_load_factor tuning are intentionally unimplemented.
how_it_is_fast: Each table position is a 14-slot chunk; F14 packs a 1-byte hash 'tag' per key into a 16-byte SIMD vector (SSE2 on x86_64, NEON on aarch64) so one vector compare filters up to 14 candidate slots per probe, letting the table run at a 12/14 max load factor with a ~1.04 average probe length on hits. Collisions resolve via double hashing with per-chunk 'overflow' reference counts standing in for tombstones, so insert/erase churn doesn't force the periodic full-table rehashes that tombstone-based open addressing needs to reclaim slots. F14ValueMap further stores entries inline in the chunk instead of behind a per-node heap allocation, which is what drives its build and iteration advantage over std::unordered_map's pointer-chasing.
when_to_use: u64 or other small trivially-copyable keys where build/insert and find throughput matter more than reference stability (F14ValueMap or F14FastMap).
Iteration-heavy workloads: F14ValueMap iterates 16x faster (u64) to 30x faster (std::string) than std::unordered_map on this harness because there's no per-node pointer chasing.
High churn workloads (caches, dedup tables, repeated insert/erase cycles) where std::unordered_map's tombstone-driven rehashes hurt.

You need std::unordered_map-compatible reference/iterator stability but still want a speed win over it: use F14NodeMap specifically (1.28x faster build+destroy, still much slower than F14ValueMap in this benchmark).
You're already building/linking Folly (or accept doing so) on x86-64/aarch64 with a C++20 toolchain.
when_not_to_use: You want a header-only, dependency-free drop-in: F14 requires building and linking libfolly, whose manifest lists ~13 external deps (boost, gflags, glog, libdwarf, libevent, libsodium, fast_float, fmt, lz4, openssl, snappy, zstd, xz) plus Linux-only libaio/libiberty/libunwind.
Targeting WebAssembly: an open folly issue (#1973) reports F14 is slower and more memory-hungry than std::unordered_map there.

Less-common platforms: open build-failure issues on ppc64le (#1838) and other powerpc targets (#2128) show threading/endianness and compile rough edges; README's platform list (Linux/macOS/Windows/iOS, x86-32/64, ARM) is not the CI-tested set.
You default to F14ValueMap/F14VectorMap/F14FastMap but need reference/iterator stability across mutation — only F14NodeMap provides that; the others may invalidate references on any insert.
Exception safety must be contractually guaranteed: an open upstream issue (#2308, filed 2024, still open) states F14's exception safety is undocumented.

integration.dependencies: boost, gflags, glog, libdwarf, libevent, libsodium, fast_float, fmt, lz4, openssl, snappy, zstd, xz (googletest for tests only); Linux additionally needs libaio, libiberty, libunwind
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2, a non-optional baseline ISA feature) and aarch64 (NEON) are the vectorized fast paths; a non-SIMD fallback exists but is untested by this benchmark. WASM and some powerpc targets have open correctness/perf issues.
integration.thread_safety: not documented beyond the same non-synchronized, single-writer-or-multiple-readers model as std::unordered_map; no built-in locking
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — F14NodeMap matches std::unordered_map's reference/iterator stability and is a safe substitute; F14ValueMap, F14VectorMap, and F14FastMap are not (no reference stability, no bucket API, max_load_factor is a no-op)

gotchas: F14ValueMap/F14VectorMap/F14FastMap may rehash before evaluating an insert's arguments, so code like map.insert(k2, map[k1]) is unsafe with them, per F14.md (same caveat as dense_hash_map and absl::flat_hash_map).

Debug and ASAN builds intentionally randomize iteration order and inject extra rehashes to expose stability bugs, so two identically-constructed maps can iterate in different orders even in the same process/build.

clear() frees all backing memory once a table has ever held >100 keys (std only requires O(size())), so a clear-and-refill loop on a table that grew large will repeatedly reallocate rather than reuse capacity.
Only F14NodeMap provides std::unordered_map's reference/iterator stability; the other three variants can move or invalidate elements on any insert.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: On this exact harness F14ValueMap is the slowest of the four SIMD hash maps compared for u64 keys: abseil's flat_hash_map (19.26 ns/op buildfree), Boost.Unordered's flat_map (23.04), and ankerl::unordered_dense (23.80) all beat F14ValueMap's 29.05, and similarly on find. Pick F14 when you're already building/linking Folly and want the ValueMap-vs-NodeMap choice between raw speed and std-compatible reference stability in one library, or need Folly's built-in heterogeneous/transparent lookup; pick a single-header sibling (unordered_dense, robin_hood) when you want the speed without Folly's ~13-dependency build.
verified_claims_summary: Read directly from martinus/unordered_dense's bench_readme.csv (clang 22.1.8, -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++20, libstdc++, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 1-2M entries): for u64 keys folly::F14ValueMap beat std::unordered_map 3.97x on build+destroy (29.05 vs 115.31 ns/op; inserts alone 2.81x, 27.98 vs 78.66), 1.72x on find (33.58 vs 57.89), 2.63x on churn (91.34 vs 240.49), and 16.35x on iteration (1.30 vs 21.29 ns/element); for std::string keys the wins were smaller on build/find/churn (1.48x/1.73x/1.62x) but iteration was 29.7x. std::unordered_map had lower peak RSS per u64 entry (45.78 B) than every SIMD/flat map tested, including F14ValueMap.
status_note: Actively maintained (commits current as of 2026-09-24, 30.5k stars, heavy internal Meta production use) under Apache-2.0, but folly gives no ABI-compatibility guarantee across commits and its own README recommends static linking and pinning a version rather than tracking main.
